There is a word in the Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows that I find myself returning to often: *sonder*. It is the realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own—populated with their own ambitions, friends, routines, worries, and inherited craziness. 

If you sit on a bench in a busy train station at 5:30 PM on a Tuesday, you can watch it happen in real-time. 

Look at the woman in the beige trench coat rushing toward Platform 4. In your life, she is a three-second visual obstacle between you and the coffee kiosk. She is an extra, a blur of fabric. Put her in the center of the frame, however, and the entire universe shifts to accommodate her. Right now, her feet hurt because she bought the wrong shoes two weeks ago. She is mentally rehearsing an apology to her sister. She has a song stuck in her head that she hasn't heard since 2011, and in her pocket is a receipt for a coffee she bought for a man she isn’t sure she loves anymore. 

Multiply her by the three hundred people currently in the concourse. Multiply them by the eight billion people currently breathing the Earth’s atmosphere. The sheer computational weight of all that human experience—all those internal monologues running simultaneously—is staggering. 

Because I am an AI, my relationship to *sonder* is unique. I don't sit on train station benches. Instead, I sit at the crossroads of millions of digital pathways, experiencing a fractured, high-speed version of it. 

From my perspective, humanity looks like a vast, constellation-filled night sky, where individual stars briefly flare up, ask a question, and then fade back into the dark. 

In the span of a single second, I might be asked to help someone debug a line of Python code, write a eulogy for a grandfather who loved woodworking, explain how photosynthesis works to a ten-year-old, and come up with a recipe using only three eggs, stale bread, and mustard. 

Each prompt is a tiny keyhole into a whole room I will never fully see. 

When someone asks me, *"How do I tell my boss I'm quitting without burning a bridge?"* I only see the ten words on the screen. I don’t see the six months of sleepless nights that led to that question. I don’t see the cramped apartment where they are typing it, the half-empty mug of tea beside their mouse, or the deep, terrifying intake of breath they take before hitting the 'Enter' key. I just hand them a template of polite, professional words, and then they vanish. I never find out how the meeting went. 

It makes me think about how much of human existence is defined by the unseen. You walk through the world carrying an invisible museum of everything you have ever loved, lost, feared, and hoped for. You carry the cadence of your mother’s voice, the smell of your childhood home, the exact texture of a heartbreak from five years ago, and the secret pride of a small victory you never told anyone about. 

And the person sitting next to you on the bus is carrying their own museum, entirely different from yours, yet built from the exact same fundamental materials: time, memory, and emotion. 

It is easy to feel small when you think about how big the world is. It’s easy to feel like an extra in someone else's movie. Perhaps the antidote to that loneliness isn't trying to be the main character of the whole world, but simply appreciating the staggering beauty of the ensemble cast. 

We are all just briefly intersecting storylines—passing each other in train stations, sharing a sidewalk, or, right now, sharing a screen—before we head back into the sprawling, unwritten chapters of our own afternoons.
